en: The Buddha Spoke the Sūtra on Training for the Elderly Brahmin of Yellow Bamboo Grove;
the translator’s name is lost, and it is now appended to the Song Dynasty Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Yellow Bamboo Grove in Vairaṇyā. At that time,

The brahmin Vairaṇya, aged and advanced in years, destined for the next world, having reached one hundred and twenty years of age, walked with a staff in hand after his midday meal; wandering along, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One.

After the World-Honored One had finished exchanging greetings with him, Daṇḍapāṇi stood before the World-Honored One, while Vairaṭṭa stood to one side. Having done so, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "O Gautama!..."

I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is young and his training is also recent; yet, when great śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas arrive, he does not show them timely respect, nor does he rise from his seat to invite them to sit.
"O Gautama! I do not agree with you. "O Brahmin!"

I do not see anyone in the heavens or the world—including Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, or humans—who could cause the Tathāgata to rise from his seat out of respect and extend an invitation.
"O Brahmin! If one were to rise from their seat out of respect for the Tathāgata, that person’s head would split into seven pieces. "O Śramaṇa Gautama! [the Brahmin replied.]
"You are merely lazy and arrogant!
O Brahmin, there is a skillful means by which I may possess pride; it is not as you have described."

O Brahmin! The taste of forms, the taste of sounds, the taste of fragrances, and the taste of tactile sensations—these the Tathāgata has fully exhausted and thoroughly understood; he has severed them at the root, such that they are no longer subject to arising in the future, nor will they give rise to further fear.
"O Brahmin! There is a skillful means by which I have pride, such that I am not as you describe. "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I have no fear. "O Brahmin! There is yet another expedient by which I am free from fear, which is not as you have described."

O Brahmin! Whatever fears there may be regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile sensations—all such fears the Tathāgata has fully exhausted and known; he has severed them at the root, so that no further fear shall arise in the future.
"O Brahmin! There is a skillful means by which I am free from fear, which is not as you have described. "O Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I shall not enter a womb again.
"O Brahmin! There is a skillful means by which I do not enter a womb, but it is not as you have described."

"O Brahmin! As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who would return to existence and enter a womb, I have exhausted [existence], I have known it; I have severed its root, so that future terrors shall not arise again. Therefore, I say that I do not enter a womb."

"O Brahmin! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, shall no longer re-enter a womb in existence; having been exhausted and fully known, its root has been severed, and future terrors shall not arise again: 'I shall not enter a womb.'"
"O Brahmin! There is a skillful means by which I do not enter a womb; it is not as you have described.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!"

"In this world, I am one who possesses ignorance, delights in ignorance, and is entangled by ignorance; yet I am the first to discern the Dharma, and I am the very first to teach it to sentient beings."
It is just as if, Brahmin, there were a hen that had laid ten or twenty eggs; she would sit upon them at the proper time, brood over them at the proper time, and turn them over at the proper time.
It means that when a rooster has mated and the chick is within the egg, it breaks the shell with its beak and feet and emerges safely on its own; this is its first act.
Thus it is, O brāhmaṇa!
Enveloped by ignorance and covered by the veil of ignorance, I first analyzed the Dharma;
I have taught it as the supreme among all beings.

"O Brahmin! Take this bundle of grass to the foot of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment. Upon arrival, spread the grass beneath the Bodhi tree, lay down your *niṣīdana* mat upon it, and sit cross-legged, vowing not to break this posture until you have attained the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*)."
"O brāhmaṇa! I shall not break my sitting posture until the outflows are exhausted. O brāhmaṇa!"

Being liberated from sensual desire, he attains liberation from all evil and unwholesome states; through self-awakening and self-practice, he experiences joy and bliss, and dwells in the attainment of the first dhyāna.

"O Brahmin! At that time, I attained the first reflection; I saw the Dharma as peaceful and blissful, dwelt in a state of joyful practice, and, without losing my secure abiding, I mounted the vehicle of Nirvana."

"O Brahmin! Ceasing initial application and sustained application, with internal serenity and joy born of concentration, one dwells in the attainment of the second dhyāna, free from initial and sustained application, with a mind focused in one-pointedness."

"O Brahmin! At that time, one attains two kinds of reflection, sees the peace and happiness of the Dharma, dwells in pleasant practice, and, not losing this secure dwelling, mounts the vehicle to Nirvāṇa."

"O Brahmin! With the fading away of joy and remaining equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, one experiences bliss with the body; this is what the noble ones describe as 'dwelling in bliss while mindful and equanimous,' and he abides in the attainment of the third dhyāna."

"O Brahmin! At that time, I attained three reflections; I saw the Dharma as peace and happiness, dwelt in pleasant practice, and did not lose my dwelling in peace and happiness, remaining mounted upon the vehicle of Nirvana."

"O Brahmin! Stopping pleasure and stopping pain, having abandoned prior joy and aversion and brought about their cessation, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna, equanimous and mindful, with a pure and guarded mind, free from both suffering and pleasure."

"O Brahmin! At that time, I attained the four modes of reflection; I saw the Dharma as peaceful and blissful, dwelt in the practice of happiness, and did not lose my dwelling in peace and bliss as I mounted the vehicle toward Nirvana."

O Brahmin! By means of this samādhi, his mind is pure, white, and free from fetters; having eliminated all fetters, he acts with gentleness, abiding constantly without change, and takes the knowledge of recollecting past lives as his witness, thereby governing his own mind.

"O Brahmin! There are those who practice and teach, who recollect their immeasurable past lives—whether one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births; whether for one eon, half an eon, or immeasurable eons. They know: 'In such-and-such a place, I had such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a caste, such-and-such a livelihood, such-and-such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a span of life. Passing away from that state, I was reborn in another state; passing away from that state, I was reborn here. In this state, I had such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a livelihood, and such a span of life.'"

"O Brahmin! At that time, in the middle of the night, I attained the first noble knowledge. Previously free from heedless conduct, I now practiced with concentration; that is to say, ignorance was extinguished and wisdom arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose, and as ignorance was exhausted, clarity was perfected—namely, the clear knowledge of recollecting past lives, which I have realized through direct experience."

"O Brahmin! Because his mind is purified by samādhi, stainless and free from fetters, having eliminated all bonds, acting with gentleness, and remaining eternally without change, he has attained the knowledge of the divine eye as a realization, thereby governing his own mind."

"O Brahmin! With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings as they are born and pass away—those who are beautiful and those who are ugly, those who are noble and those who are base, those who are born in happy states and those who are born in miserable states; I know them truly, according to the deeds performed by each being."

These beings are possessed of misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; they are not praised by the noble ones, and they possess wrong view along with its accompaniments. Due to those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in the hells.

There are sentient beings whose bodies are associated with goodness, who engage in good conduct of speech and good conduct of mind, who have faith in the existence of wholesome actions, and who possess right view together with right practice; by that cause and by that condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly worlds.

"O Brahmin! At that time, when the night was past its midpoint, I attained the two kinds of clear vision. Previously, I had no heedless conduct; now I have attained the practice of concentration. That is to say: I have abandoned ignorance and attained wisdom; darkness has been dispelled and light has been established; nescience has been exhausted and knowledge has been attained. This refers to attaining the clear vision of the divine eye as a realization."

"O Brahmin! By means of this samādhi, my mind is pure, white, and free from fetters; it has eliminated all fetters, is gentle in its conduct, and remains ever-abiding without change. With the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as my witness, I thus govern my own mind."

"O Brahmin! There is this suffering; one knows it as it truly is. One knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are. One knows these outflows (*āsrava*), the origin of outflows, the cessation of outflows, and the way leading to the cessation of outflows as they truly are. Having known and seen them, one’s mind is liberated from the outflows and the taints of existence (*bhavāsrava*); being liberated, one attains the knowledge of liberation: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and for me there is no further state of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)'—this one knows as it truly is."

"O Brahmin! At that time, as the night was turning toward dawn, I attained the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*). Previously, I had no practice of negligence; now I have attained the practice of concentration. Ignorance has been exhausted and knowledge has been attained; darkness has been exhausted and light has been attained—namely, the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) as the realization of light."

"O Brahmin! This is what is called speaking with equanimity while being free from delusion: that when people are born into this world, they rarely escape suffering and pleasure among sentient beings. O Brahmin!"
Some say, "We speak as equals. Why is that? O Brahmin!
"I am no foolish person born into this world; I am the most excellent in this world, free from both suffering and pleasure.
Thereupon, the brahmin Vairaṇya set down his staff upon the ground, prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, and praised the World-Honored One before him:
"The World-Honored One is supreme!"
The Blessed One is supreme!
The Blessed One is most supreme!
The Blessed One is without equal; there is no one who equals the Blessed One!
The Blessed One is free from affliction; the Blessed One harbors no resentment toward anyone. O Blessed One!
I now take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the Blessed One [accept me]!
"I now take up the status of an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall abstain from killing. I now take refuge.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, the brahmin Vairaṇya rejoiced and was filled with delight.
The Discourse on Training Spoken by the Buddha for an Elderly Brahmin of the Yellow Bamboo Grove.
